steps.title: Zero, root, \(x\)-intercept: one thing, three names
steps.body:
A zero of \(f\) is a value of \(x\) with \(f(x)=0\):
•  on the graph, it is where the curve crosses (or touches) the \(x\)-axis
•  “the roots of \(f(x)=0\)” and “the \(x\)-intercepts of \(y=f(x)\)” mean the same values
•  the \(y\)-coordinate is always \(0\), so the answer is just the \(x\)-value(s)

Not to be confused with the \(y\)-intercept, \(f(0)\): here \(f(0)=1\).

steps.title: Which of these is NOT asking for the zeros of \(f\)?
opts: Find the \(y\)-intercept of the graph of \(f\)
Find where the graph of \(f\) crosses the \(x\)-axis
steps.ok: ✓ Right. The \(y\)-intercept is \(f(0)\); the other two are the zeros.
bads: ✗ “Solve \(f(x)=0\)” is exactly the zeros. The odd one out is the \(y\)-intercept, \(f(0)\).
✗ Crossing the \(x\)-axis is exactly the zeros. The odd one out is the \(y\)-intercept, \(f(0)\).

steps.title: Finding every zero

nspire.body:
The tool finds one zero at a time, between the bounds you give it. To be sure you have them all:
•  a polynomial of degree \(n\) has at most \(n\) zeros: a cubic, up to three
•  the curve must cross the axis between your two bounds; put them close around one crossing
•  a zero where the curve only touches the axis (no sign change) is a repeated root: the Nspire’s Zero tool wants a crossing between the two bounds; a touching zero can be found with Analyze Graph → Minimum (or Maximum) instead.

ti84.body:
The tool finds one zero at a time, between the bounds you give it. To be sure you have them all:
•  a polynomial of degree \(n\) has at most \(n\) zeros: a cubic, up to three
•  the curve must cross the axis between your two bounds; put them close around one crossing
•  a zero where the curve only touches the axis (no sign change) is a repeated root: the TI-84’s zero tool needs a sign change between Left Bound and Right Bound; for a touching zero use CALC → 3: minimum (or 4: maximum) instead.

cg50.body:

•  the curve must cross the axis between your two bounds; put them close around one crossing
•  a zero where the curve only touches the axis (no sign change) is a repeated root: the Casio’s ROOT usually finds a touching zero; if it does not, use G-Solv → MIN (or MAX) instead.

steps.title: Any equation is a zero problem
steps.body:
To solve \(x^{3}=5x-1\), move everything to one side: \(x^{3}-5x+1=0\). The solutions are the zeros of \(f(x)=x^{3}-5x+1\).
•  one graph instead of two, and the zero tool instead of intersection
•  either method is accepted; use the one you find quicker
•  “show that there is a root between \(2\) and \(3\)”: show a sign change, \(f(2)<0\) and \(f(3)>0\), then find it

“When does the ball hit the ground?” means \(h(t)=0\): a zero of \(h\).
•  the model may give a zero that makes no sense (negative time, negative length): reject it, and say why
•  give units: \(t=4.07\) seconds
•  the domain of the story is your window: here \(t\ge0\)

steps.title: How do you find the other zeros without a calculator?
opts: \(x=2\) is a zero, so \((x-2)\) is a factor: divide to get \(x^{2}-4x+1\), then the quadratic formula
